_note: Spoken guide scripts, one per destination slug. Recorded English lives in media/audio/guide-<slug>.mp3, other languages in guide_scripts.<lang>.json and guide-<slug>.<lang>.mp3. voice_guides.py records only what is missing, so this file is the queue and the archive at once. Write for the ear: short sentences, one story worth repeating, one instruction the traveller can act on. Two to three minutes of speech, about 1,200 to 1,800 characters. Numbers are spelled out because the reader says digits badly.
pike-place-market: Pike Place Market. This is the oldest continuously running farmers market in the country, open since nineteen oh seven, and it started as a protest. Onion prices had jumped tenfold in a season, so the city gave farmers a strip of planking above the waterfront and told them to sell straight to the public, no middleman. That rule survives. Almost every stall you pass is still the person who grew it, caught it, baked it or made it, which is why the prices make sense and the answers do too. Ask the woman with the peaches where they came from and she will name the orchard and the week. The fish throwers at the corner counter are the show everybody films, and it is worth watching once. Then walk away from it, because the market is nine acres and four levels deep, and almost nobody goes down. Under the main arcade there are magic shops, map dealers, a tiny record store and the old comic stall, and the crowds thin with every staircase. The first Starbucks is across the cobbles at nineteen twelve Pike Place, and the line is usually forty minutes for coffee you can buy anywhere. Your call. One practical thing. Come before ten in the morning if you want photographs and flowers, come at noon if you want to eat, and do not come by car. The garage below fills by nine thirty on a weekend and the hill back up is steeper than it looks. Give this place two hours. It will take three.
the-met-museum: The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Five thousand years of human making under one roof on the edge of Central Park, and the honest advice comes first: nobody sees it all. Two million objects, two million square feet. Visitors who try to walk everything leave exhausted and remember nothing. Pick two wings and walk them slowly. That is the whole strategy. If you take one thing, take the Temple of Dendur. It is a real Egyptian temple, two thousand years old, that stood on the bank of the Nile until the Aswan dam was built and the water was going to swallow it. Egypt gave it to the United States for helping to rescue the monuments, and it was shipped here in six hundred and sixty one crates and rebuilt stone by stone in a hall of glass facing the park. In the late afternoon the light comes across the reflecting pool and hits sandstone that was quarried before Rome. The American Wing courtyard is the quietest good room in the building. The arms and armour hall is the one children never want to leave. And in summer the roof garden is open with a skyline view that most visitors never find, because it is not on the way to anything. Two practical notes. The admission price is a suggestion for New York State residents and students from three neighbouring states, and a fixed ticket for everyone else, so have that ready. And the Fifth Avenue steps are the meeting point for the whole city, which means if you get separated, that is where you go. Give it three hours and it will still be the fastest three hours of the trip.
staten-island-ferry: The Staten Island Ferry. This is the best free thing in New York and it is not close. Twenty five minutes across the harbour, no ticket, no booking, running twenty four hours a day, every day of the year, because it is not a tour. It is the commute. Thirty five thousand people ride it to work, which is exactly why it is still free and still frequent. You leave from Whitehall Terminal at the bottom of Manhattan. As the boat pulls out you get the whole financial district skyline pulling away behind you, then Governors Island, then the Statue of Liberty about a quarter mile off the starboard side, close enough to see her face, followed by Ellis Island where twelve million people entered this country. Here is the part most visitors get wrong. Stand on the right hand side going out toward Staten Island, which is the starboard side, for the statue. Coming back, stand at the front for the skyline, because the return run into Manhattan at dusk with the towers lighting up is the shot everybody wants and half of them are facing the wrong way. At the far end you must get off the boat and walk back around through the terminal to reboard. It takes about five minutes and it is signposted, but if you stay in your seat you will be asked to leave anyway. Budget an hour and a quarter door to door and bring something warm. That harbour wind does not care what the forecast said.
space-needle: The Space Needle. Six hundred and five feet, built in about four hundred days for the nineteen sixty two World's Fair, and the whole thing began as a sketch on a napkin in a coffee house. The designer wanted a tethered balloon. The committee wanted a flying saucer. What you are looking at is the argument they settled on. The foundation is the part worth knowing. They dug a hole thirty feet deep and poured four hundred and sixty seven concrete trucks in a single continuous day, the largest pour in the West at the time, and the foundation now weighs about the same as the tower standing on it. That is why it does not move much. It is built to take a wind of two hundred miles an hour and an earthquake of nine point one, and it has ridden out everything the region has thrown at it since. Up top the observation deck was rebuilt with floor to ceiling glass and open air glass benches that lean you out over the drop. The floor below is the Loupe, the world's only revolving glass floor. It turns slowly enough that you notice it only when you look down and the city has moved. One honest piece of advice. This is a clear day attraction. On a grey Seattle afternoon you are paying to stand inside a cloud. Check the mountain first: if you can see Rainier from the street, go up now. If you cannot, spend the money at Chihuly next door and come back tomorrow. And book a timed ticket, because the walk up queue on a sunny weekend runs past an hour.
bainbridge-island-ferry: The Bainbridge Island ferry. Thirty five minutes each way across Puget Sound, and it is the cheapest good hour in Seattle. You pay only going west, walk on for a few dollars, and the ride home is free, so a round trip costs you one fare and about ninety minutes. Go up to the outside deck as soon as you board and stay there. Leaving Colman Dock you get the downtown skyline stacked against the hills with the Space Needle off to the right, and on a clear day Mount Rainier standing behind the whole city looking close enough to touch, which it is not. It is sixty miles away and fourteen thousand feet tall. That is the thing locals mean when they say the mountain is out. Look ahead and the Olympic range fills the far shore. This is a working ferry, one of the busiest in the country, carrying islanders with groceries and dogs and bicycles, so it runs in fog and it runs in rain. The rain does not stop it and it should not stop you. Wet weather on this crossing has its own quality, with the islands going soft and grey and the gulls riding the wake right at the rail. At the far end, Winslow is a ten minute walk up from the dock, a single main street with a good bookshop, a bakery, and a handful of places to eat looking back at the water. Give yourself an hour there and catch the boat back at sunset. Check the sailing time before you walk up. Miss it and the next one can be an hour.
lincoln-memorial: The Lincoln Memorial. Thirty six columns, one for each state in the Union when Lincoln died, and the man himself sitting nineteen feet high in Georgia marble. The sculptor Daniel Chester French worked on it for four years. Look at the hands. The left is clenched, the right is open and relaxed, and people have argued for a century about whether he carved the letters A and L in sign language into them. The family always said no. Visitors keep seeing it anyway. Read the walls, because the walls are the memorial. On the south side is the Gettysburg Address, two hundred and seventy two words that took about two minutes to deliver and that the newspapers of the day called a failure. On the north is the Second Inaugural, given one month before he was killed, with the line about malice toward none and charity for all carved where anyone can stand and read it. Then turn around and find the spot on the steps. Eighteen steps down from the chamber there is an inscription in the stone marking where Martin Luther King junior stood on the twenty eighth of August nineteen sixty three and told a quarter of a million people about a dream, with Lincoln directly behind him. It is a small engraved line and most people walk over it. Come at night if you can. The memorial never closes, it is lit from within, the crowds are gone, and the reflecting pool holds the Washington Monument upside down all the way to the far end. Twenty minutes here is enough. It will stay with you longer than that.
empire-state-building: The Empire State Building. One thousand four hundred and fifty four feet to the tip, built in one year and forty five days during the Great Depression, at a pace of about four and a half floors a week. Three thousand four hundred workers, many of them Mohawk ironworkers from Kahnawake who walked the beams without harnesses. It came in ahead of schedule and under budget, which has essentially never happened since. It opened in nineteen thirty one to an empty city. Nobody could afford the offices, so New Yorkers called it the Empty State Building for years, and it survived on ticket money from people paying to go up. The observatory kept it alive. In nineteen forty five a B twenty five bomber lost in fog flew into the seventy ninth floor. Fourteen people died, and the building was open for business again on Monday. There are two decks. The eighty sixth is the one you want, outdoors, open air, with the wind and the sound of the city coming up at you. The hundred and second is glassed in, higher, and costs more, and on most days it does not give you enough extra to be worth it. Timing decides everything here. Sunset is the most crowded hour of the day. Go at eight in the morning when it opens and you will share it with almost nobody, or go after ten at night when the last families have gone and the grid below is fully lit. Book a timed ticket either way, and know that the tower lights change colour for holidays and causes, so whatever colour it is tonight, it means something.
central-park: Central Park. Eight hundred and forty three acres in the middle of Manhattan, and none of it is natural. Every hill, lake, meadow and outcrop was designed and built by hand between eighteen fifty seven and eighteen seventy six. Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux moved nearly three million cubic yards of soil and rock and planted something like four million trees and shrubs on what had been swamp and stone. It is one of the largest works of landscape art in the world, and it is pretending to be a place that just happened. Look for the four transverse roads that carry traffic across the park. Olmsted sank them below the sight lines so a crosstown bus would never interrupt the view from a footpath. That single decision is why the park still feels like countryside a hundred and fifty years later. If you have one hour, walk the Mall under the elms, cross Bethesda Terrace to the fountain, and go up to Bow Bridge. That is the postcard, and it earns it. If you have two, add the Ramble behind the lake, thirty six acres of deliberately confusing woodland where people go to get lost on purpose and where the birdwatchers gather during migration. Practical points. The park is bigger than it looks on a map, over two and a half miles top to bottom, so pick a gate and a direction rather than trying to cross it. The lamp posts have four digit numbers on them: the first two digits are the nearest street, which is how you find yourself when you are lost. And it is free, always, all of it.
brooklyn-bridge: The Brooklyn Bridge. Opened in eighteen eighty three, the first steel wire suspension bridge in the world, and for twenty years the longest span on earth. It cost fifteen million dollars and at least twenty seven lives, and the story of who finished it is the reason to walk it. John Roebling designed it and died of tetanus before construction began, after a ferry crushed his foot while he was surveying the site. His son Washington took over and was paralysed by decompression sickness from working in the pressurised caissons dug into the riverbed. So Emily Roebling, Washington's wife, learned the mathematics, the cable specifications and the engineering, and ran the project for eleven years, carrying her husband's instructions to the site while he watched through a telescope from their window in Brooklyn Heights. She was the first person to cross it. The public did not trust it. Six days after it opened, a rumour that it was collapsing caused a stampede that killed twelve people. So the next year P T Barnum walked twenty one elephants across it, and that settled the argument. Walk it from Brooklyn toward Manhattan, not the other way. That direction puts the skyline in front of you the whole crossing instead of behind your shoulder. It is about a mile and takes thirty to forty minutes with stops. Stay in the pedestrian lane and out of the bike lane, because those cyclists are commuting and they are fast. Early morning light is the good light, and it is also the only hour the walkway is not shoulder to shoulder.
9-11-memorial-and-museum: The National September Eleventh Memorial. Two square voids set exactly in the footprints of the towers that stood here, each an acre, with water falling thirty feet down all four sides into a second, smaller void at the centre that you cannot see the bottom of. The architect Michael Arad called the design Reflecting Absence, and the point is that the emptiness is kept, not filled. The names of two thousand nine hundred and seventy seven people killed here, at the Pentagon, in Shanksville, and in the nineteen ninety three bombing are cut through the bronze parapets. They are not alphabetical. They are arranged by what the memorial calls meaningful adjacencies: colleagues beside colleagues, first responders beside their companies, friends beside friends, from requests the families made. People who died together are together. Look for the Survivor Tree on the plaza. A Callery pear pulled from the rubble in October two thousand and one, eight feet of burned trunk with one living branch. It was nursed back in a Bronx nursery for nine years and replanted here. It is now taller than the buildings around the plaza edge, and every spring it flowers before the other trees. The plaza is free and open. The museum below is ticketed and takes two hours and it is heavy, so decide honestly whether you want that today. Whichever you choose, this is a burial ground for many of the people named here. Speak quietly. On a birthday the staff place a white rose in that person's name.
grand-central-terminal: Grand Central Terminal. Not station, terminal, because the tracks end here. Forty four platforms and sixty seven tracks on two levels, the most of any railway station in the world, all of it buried under the street so that Park Avenue could be built on top. That was the deal that paid for the building in nineteen thirteen: bury the trains, sell the air. Stand in the middle of the main concourse and look up. The ceiling is the night sky, twenty five hundred stars, sixty of them lit, and it is backwards. The constellations are reversed, as if you were looking down at the sky from outside it rather than up from the ground. The official explanation is that it was painted from a medieval manuscript that showed the heavens from God's point of view. The likelier explanation is that somebody flipped the drawing. The family who commissioned it declined to fix it. There is one small dark rectangle near the crab of Cancer. That is the original grime, left uncleaned in the nineteen nineties restoration so visitors could see what decades of tobacco smoke had done to the whole ceiling. Go down the ramp to the Oyster Bar and find the four low arches outside the door. Stand facing into one corner while a friend faces into the opposite one, twenty feet away, and whisper. The tiled vault carries your voice straight to them and to nobody in between. It works every time, it costs nothing, and half the people walking past have no idea it is there.
the-high-line: The High Line. A mile and a half of freight railway thirty feet above the West Side, built in the nineteen thirties to get trains off the street after so many people were killed at level crossings that Tenth Avenue was called Death Avenue. The last train ran in nineteen eighty carrying three carloads of frozen turkeys, and then the line sat abandoned for twenty five years while the property owners below tried to have it torn down. What saved it was that it had gone wild. Seeds blew in, and a self sown meadow of grasses and birch grew up in the ballast between the rails, thirty feet in the air, in the middle of Manhattan. A photographer spent a year documenting it, two neighbours founded a group to protect it, and the planting you walk through today is a deliberate echo of that accident, with about half the species native to the region. Walk it from Gansevoort Street at the south end and go north. You pass through buildings, not just between them, and the section at Tenth Avenue drops you into a sunken amphitheatre with a window looking straight down the avenue at the traffic, which is the best free seat in the neighbourhood. It is a linear park, so there are limited entrances and most have stairs, with lifts at Gansevoort, Fourteenth, Twenty third and Thirtieth. Budget forty five minutes end to end without stops, and more like ninety with them. Go early or go at dusk, because the middle of a summer afternoon up there is a slow moving queue with no shade.
times-square: Times Square. Let us be honest about what this is. It is an advertising space that became a landmark, and roughly three hundred and thirty thousand people pass through it every day. New Yorkers avoid it. You should still see it once, at night, for about twenty minutes. It was Longacre Square, the carriage trade district, until the New York Times moved its headquarters here in nineteen oh four and the city renamed it. The paper celebrated with a fireworks display on New Year's Eve, and when fireworks were later banned they lowered an illuminated ball down the flagpole instead. That was nineteen oh seven. It has happened almost every year since, and it is why a million people stand in the cold here each December. By the nineteen seventies it had become the most dangerous block in the city. The clean up that followed was so complete that the zoning now legally requires the illuminated signs. Every landlord on the square must maintain a certain brightness. The glare is not an accident, it is code, and at night the light is strong enough to read a newspaper by at one in the morning. Practical advice, and take this seriously. The costumed characters are not employees of anyone and they will ask for money after the photograph, so agree the price first or do not pose. The red steps above the TKTS booth are free and the best place to sit and watch. And the restaurants on the square are the worst value in the city, so eat one street away in any direction.
chihuly-garden-and-glass: Chihuly Garden and Glass. Dale Chihuly grew up in Tacoma an hour south of here and changed what glass could be. This is the permanent collection at the foot of the Space Needle, eight galleries and a glasshouse and a garden, and it is the rare attraction that is better in bad weather. The centrepiece is the Glasshouse, a hundred foot long room under a curved glass roof, with a suspended sculpture forty three feet long in reds, oranges and yellows hanging overhead. When the Seattle sky is flat grey, that colour overhead is the entire point. Outside in the garden the glass forms are planted among real plants so that you keep having to look twice to work out which is which, and when it rains the pieces bead with water and get better. Chihuly lost the sight in his left eye in a car accident in nineteen seventy six and dislocated a shoulder bodysurfing three years later, so he stopped blowing glass himself. He directs teams now. He described it as being more choreographer than dancer, and the work got larger and more ambitious after he stopped holding the pipe. It takes about an hour, a little more if you sit in the Glasshouse, which you should. Combined tickets with the Space Needle next door cost less than buying both separately. And if the mountain is hidden and the Needle is pointless today, this is the answer: it is indoors, it is fifty yards away, and the weather cannot touch it.
gas-works-park: Gas Works Park. This was a coal gasification plant that ran from nineteen oh six to nineteen fifty six, making the gas that lit Seattle's streetlamps, and when it closed the site was a poisoned twenty acre ruin on the best waterfront in the city. Everyone assumed the towers would come down. The landscape architect Richard Haag spent months on the site and argued the opposite: keep the machinery. It was a genuinely radical idea in nineteen seventy, that industrial wreckage could be beautiful rather than shameful, and the city fought him. He won. The cracking towers still stand rusted at the north end, and the old exhauster compressor building was painted and turned into a play barn where children climb the actual machines. He also pioneered the cleanup. Rather than digging out the contaminated ground he used bioremediation, seeding the soil with organisms to digest the hydrocarbons in place. It was one of the first uses of that approach anywhere and it is standard practice now. Climb the Great Mound, the grass hill at the water's edge. On top there is a bronze and concrete sundial that uses your own shadow as the pointer, so you stand on the marked spot and read the time off your body. From up there you get the full downtown skyline straight across Lake Union with float planes landing in front of it. It is the best free view in Seattle, it is a working neighbourhood park, and on the fourth of July it is the place the whole city goes.
kerry-park-viewpoint: Kerry Park. This is a strip of pavement and grass about the size of a tennis court, and it is the single most photographed spot in Seattle. Every postcard, every establishing shot in every film set here, was taken from where you are standing. It was given to the city in nineteen twenty seven by Albert and Katharine Kerry so that, in their words, all who stop here may enjoy this view. The composition is why it works. The Space Needle sits in the middle distance at the right height, downtown stacks up behind it, Elliott Bay runs across the bottom of the frame, and on a clear day Mount Rainier floats above the whole thing to the south, sixty miles away and looking like a matte painting. Nothing else in the city lines all four of those up at once. Come at dusk, about twenty minutes after sunset, when the sky still has colour in it and the office towers have switched their lights on. That is the twenty minute window everybody is here for, so expect a row of tripods and be gracious about it. Sunrise is nearly empty and the light comes from behind the city, which is harder but quieter. Two practical notes. This is a residential street on the south slope of Queen Anne with almost no parking and neighbours who have lived with the crowds for decades, so keep your voice down after dark. And there is nothing here but the view. Ten minutes is the whole visit, so pair it with something else on the hill.
museum-of-pop-culture: The Museum of Pop Culture, MoPOP. You will have opinions about the building before you get to the door. Frank Gehry designed it, and he began by buying several Fender Stratocasters, cutting them apart, and using the pieces as the model for the shape. Twenty one thousand shingles in gold, silver, red, blue and purple, no two curved panels the same. It has been called a smashed guitar and worse. It is also unmistakably itself, and the monorail runs straight through the middle of it. Paul Allen founded it, and it started as a shrine to one man. Jimi Hendrix was from Seattle, and Allen's collection of his instruments and handwritten lyrics is the seed the rest grew around. Nirvana came next, then the whole grunge story, told in the city that made it, with Kurt Cobain's guitars and the flyers off the telephone poles. It has since widened to science fiction, horror and fantasy, which is where it gets fun: original props, costumes and manuscripts, and a horror gallery that is genuinely effective in the dark. Upstairs the Sound Lab gives you real instruments in soundproof rooms and nobody watching, so you can pick up a drum kit or a guitar and be terrible in private for as long as you want. Give it two hours. It is indoors, it is next to the Space Needle and Chihuly, and the three of them together make a full grey day without ever going outside for more than a minute.
seattle-aquarium: The Seattle Aquarium, on Pier fifty nine right over the water it studies. That is the thing that makes it different from most aquariums. The animals here are largely from Puget Sound, a few hundred feet away, and the water in the tanks is pumped in from under the pier. Start at the Window on Washington Waters, a twenty foot wide tank holding eighteen thousand gallons of Neah Bay, with rockfish and salmon and anemones, and divers who go in and talk to you through a microphone several times a day. The Underwater Dome comes next, a glass room with three hundred and sixty degrees of fish circling above and around you. Find the giant Pacific octopus. It is the largest octopus species in the world, it can span twenty feet, it has nine brains and three hearts, and roughly two thirds of its neurons are in its arms, so each arm partly thinks for itself. They are also famous escape artists and problem solvers, which is why the lids are latched. Every year around Valentine's Day the aquarium introduces a male and a female in public and lets the city watch. The sea otters are the crowd, and they are here for a reason: they were hunted to local extinction for their fur, which is the densest of any animal, up to a million hairs per square inch, and the Washington population today descends from fifty nine animals relocated from Alaska in nineteen sixty nine. Ninety minutes covers it, and it is a short flat walk from Pike Place Market.
starbucks-reserve-roastery: The Starbucks Reserve Roastery on Capitol Hill. Ignore the sign for a moment. This is a fifteen thousand square foot working coffee factory that you are allowed to walk around inside, and it happens to have bars in it. The copper cask in the middle holds green coffee that gets roasted on site in the drums along the wall, and after roasting the beans travel overhead through clear tubes to the bars, so you can literally watch your coffee move to the counter. The symbols stamped into the cask are a made up language that spells out the roasting process, which is either charming or too much depending on your mood. The reason to come is that they brew things here that no ordinary Starbucks does. Single origin lots in small quantities, siphon vacuum brewers, cold brew on nitrogen tap, and a machine called the Clover that brews one cup at a time under vacuum. Ask the person behind the bar what came in this week and let them choose for you. They are trained to talk about it and almost nobody asks. Princi bakes on site, so the food is real, and the upstairs bar serves coffee cocktails in the evening. Two honest notes. It is expensive, several times the price of the shop on the corner, and it is busy from mid morning until late. Go on a weekday before ten and you will have the roasting floor nearly to yourself. And it is a fifteen minute walk uphill from downtown, which is worth knowing before you set off in the rain.
washington-monument: The Washington Monument. Five hundred and fifty five feet of marble, the tallest stone structure in the world, and if you look about a third of the way up you will see the stone change colour. That line is the story. Construction began in eighteen forty eight and stopped in eighteen fifty four when the money ran out and the political society that had seized control of the project stalled it. The stump stood unfinished through the Civil War, a hundred and fifty feet of abandoned masonry with cattle grazing at the base. Mark Twain called it a factory chimney with the top broken off. Work restarted in eighteen seventy nine, twenty five years later, and the quarry that had supplied the original marble could no longer match it. So the tower is two different stones and always will be. It was finished in eighteen eighty four with a nine inch aluminium cap, which at the time was a precious metal more expensive than silver. It was displayed in a jewellery shop window before being carried up. There is an elevator to the observation level at five hundred feet with a window on each side: the Capitol east, the Lincoln Memorial west, the White House north, the Jefferson south. Tickets are free but they are timed and they go fast, released online at ten in the morning the day before, and the walk up queue is small. Get one in advance or plan to admire it from the grass, which is genuinely fine. The best view of Washington does not include the monument, and this is the one place you cannot see it from.
jefferson-memorial: The Jefferson Memorial, across the Tidal Basin, and it is the one people skip because it is a walk. Take the walk. It is modelled on the Pantheon in Rome, which Jefferson admired and borrowed from for his own house at Monticello and for the rotunda at the University of Virginia, so the building is quoting the man's own taste back at him. Inside, a nineteen foot bronze stands looking out across the water at the White House. The four panels on the walls are his words, and the fourth is the one to read. Laws and institutions must go hand in hand with the progress of the human mind, he wrote. As new discoveries are made, institutions must advance also, and keep pace with the times. It is an argument, carved in stone, against treating anything as finished. The memorial was controversial when it was built in the nineteen thirties. Cherry trees had to be moved for it and women chained themselves to the trees in protest, which is why the planting around it is now so carefully protected. For two weeks each spring, those trees, a gift from Tokyo in nineteen twelve, turn the whole basin pink and this becomes the most crowded quarter mile in the city. Come at sunrise. The light comes across the water straight into the columns, the joggers are the only company, and the reflection of the dome in the basin is the reason photographers set an alarm. It is about a twenty minute walk from the Lincoln Memorial around the water, and there is no closer parking, so plan the legs.
lincoln-memorial-steps: The steps of the Lincoln Memorial. Stop here before you go up, because this particular stair is a place in its own right. Eighteen steps down from the chamber, on the landing, there is an inscription cut into the granite: I have a dream. Martin Luther King junior stood on this spot on the twenty eighth of August nineteen sixty three and spoke to a quarter of a million people filling the ground from here to the Washington Monument, with Lincoln at his back and the century since emancipation in front of him. The engraving was added in two thousand and three. It is small and flush with the stone and most visitors walk straight over it. Twenty four years earlier the contralto Marian Anderson sang here on Easter Sunday to seventy five thousand people, after the Daughters of the American Revolution refused to let her perform in Constitution Hall because she was black. Eleanor Roosevelt resigned from that organisation over it and helped arrange this instead. Anderson opened with My Country, Tis of Thee. King was ten years old and listening on the radio. So stand on the landing and turn around before you turn back. The view down the reflecting pool to the monument is the view from the lectern, and the reason this became the country's gathering place is right in front of you: it is the one spot in Washington where a very large number of people can see one person and hear them. Then go up and read the walls.
air-and-space-museum: The National Air and Space Museum. This is the one where the objects are the actual objects, not replicas, and that is worth keeping in mind as you walk. The Wright Flyer hanging here is the machine from Kitty Hawk, the one that flew on the seventeenth of December nineteen oh three for twelve seconds. The Spirit of St Louis is the aircraft Charles Lindbergh flew alone across the Atlantic in thirty three and a half hours in nineteen twenty seven, with no forward windscreen, because they put a fuel tank there instead and he used a periscope. The Apollo eleven command module Columbia is the capsule that carried three men to the moon and back and splashed down in the Pacific. You can see the scorch on it. There is a piece of moon rock you are allowed to put your finger on, brought back by Apollo seventeen in nineteen seventy two and polished smooth by millions of hands since. It is about three point eight billion years old. Sixty eight years separate the Wright Flyer from the lunar module. One human lifetime, from a wood and canvas machine that flew the length of a passenger jet, to men walking on another world. Those two objects are in the same building, and the museum is arranged so you feel that. It is free, like all the Smithsonians, but timed entry passes are required and they are released online in advance. Get one before you come. Two hours minimum, and the planetarium and the flight simulators cost extra.
national-gallery-of-art: The National Gallery of Art. It is free, it is always free, and that was a condition rather than an accident. Andrew Mellon gave his collection and the money for the building to the nation in nineteen thirty seven on the terms that it would never carry his name and never charge admission, so that later collectors would not feel they were adding to one man's monument. It worked. Others gave, and the collection now runs from the thirteenth century to now. The one object to find is in the West Building: Ginevra de Benci by Leonardo da Vinci. It is the only painting by Leonardo in the Americas, there are fewer than twenty in the world, and it is a portrait of a sixteen year old Florentine woman with a juniper bush behind her head, which is a pun on her name. The bottom of the panel was cut off at some point in its history, so her hands are missing. On the back, painted to be seen, is a wreath and the motto beauty adorns virtue. Then walk the underground concourse to the East Building, which is Ieoh Ming Pei's sharp geometry of triangles, with a Calder mobile turning slowly in the atrium and modern work upstairs. The moving walkway between the two buildings passes under a ceiling of light, which children like more than most of the art. arlington-national-cemetery: Arlington National Cemetery. Six hundred and thirty nine acres, more than four hundred thousand graves, and about twenty five funerals still held here every weekday. This is an active cemetery, not a monument, and the rules of behaviour follow from that. The land was Robert E Lee's home. His wife inherited it, and when Lee left to command the Confederate army the Union took the estate and, in eighteen sixty four, began burying the war dead in the rose garden beside the house, deliberately, so the family could never return to live there. They started with the ground closest to the front door. Go to the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. A sentinel from the Third Infantry Regiment has guarded it without pause since nineteen thirty seven, through hurricanes and blizzards and every night of every year. The routine is exact: twenty one steps, a turn, twenty one seconds facing the tomb, and back, the count matching the twenty one gun salute. The changing of the guard happens every hour in winter and every half hour in summer, and it is silent. The Kennedy grave with its eternal flame is on the slope below Arlington House, and from that terrace you get the view down over the river to the Lincoln Memorial and the city.
